reading.body:
New Jersey discloses power capacity for only 5 of its 48 mapped data centers, making CyrusOne Totowa's 6 MW specification rare but modest within the state's 111.3 MW announced footprint.

Sparse disclosure is the binding constraint on understanding regional compute infrastructure. Of 48 facilities in New Jersey, operators have published IT capacity specs for just five. This gap means the state's actual power footprint, grid strain, and available headroom for AI workloads remain largely unknown. CyrusOne Totowa itself, at 6 MW, accounts for 5.4% of the disclosed total. Whether the undisclosed 43 facilities run empty, hold sensitive load data, or represent genuine capacity is unknowable from operator pages alone.

Totowa sits in the densest data center region in the United States. Power access and grid headroom are heavily contested here. A 6 MW facility is small by hyperscale standards but material to the state's grid planning. The lack of transparency across most facilities makes it impossible to assess whether New Jersey's grid can sustain the compute density this region needs or whether operators are already constrained by power availability rather than demand.
